abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are evolving from research assistants into end-to-end executors, yet their capacity to generate conclusions at scale outpaces rigorous verification. Here we introduce an auditability-centred paradigm for scientific automation, wherein trust relies not on generative capability or self-evaluation, but on whether claims can be independently traced to primary evidence, reviewed and corrected. Moving beyond post-hoc checks, we embed verification throughout the research lifecycle via four principles: grounded knowledge, bounded execution, evidence-backed results and independent verification. We instantiate this paradigm in EvoTrace for viral evolutionary analysis. Distilling peer-review critiques and methodological literature, we curated 13 principles, 236 pitfalls and 50 analytical units - validating 47 across a six-tier hierarchy - to encode methodological limits as executable constraints. Across simulated benchmarks, six viral datasets and an end-to-end Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) study, claim-evidence auditing compiled evidence packages for all 233 analyses (flagging 26 incomplete evidentiary chains), while independent numerical and figure audits rectified 17 flaws, including three blocker-level errors. For CCHFV, EvoTrace intercepted a data-contradictory claim, recalibrating 'no reassortment candidates' to 'no high-confidence candidates'. By co-delivering verification evidence, auditable automation shifts AI-driven science from autonomous generation to continuous scrutiny and correction.
